newsitem.title: CUBA: Cuba mounts diplomatic offensive in Latin America.
newsitem.headline: Cuba mounts diplomatic offensive in Latin America.

text.p: Cuban Vice President Carlos Lage met with Chile's President Eduardo Frei on Thursday on a diplomatic drive for Latin American support against moves by the United States to toughen its trade embargo on Cuba.
"We could say that rejection of the tightening of the blockade is common and unanimous in Latin America and the world," Lage said after meeting Frei.
"We've come to explain the need for Latin America to unite against the tightening of the blockade," he told reporters.

Cuban President Fidel Castro has dispatched senior aides on a tour of Latin American nations to muster help in opposing the latest moves by the Republican-controled U.S. Congress to further isolate Cuba's Communist government.
Lage, Foreign Minister Roberto Robaina and Investment Minister Ibrahim Ferradaz were sent to hand over letters from Castro to Latin leaders complaining about the U.S. moves.

Lage won only a bland repetition of Chile's opposition to the Helms-Burton Act, which seeks to discourage foreign investment in Cuba by punishing firms using property seized by Castro's government since the revolution he led in 1959.

"Our position is well-known. We've rejected it on repeated occasions, and we will do the same with any effort to harden it," said Foreign Minister Jose Miguel Insulza, referring to Helms-Burton. The law also has been criticised by Washington's allies in Europe and North America.
Lage met with Uruguayan President Julio Sanguinetti on Tuesday, Argentine President Carlos Menem on Wednesday.
Cuban Foreign Minister Roberto Robaina, meanwhile, has been meeting Caribbean and Central American leaders.

Robaina met Mexican President Ernesto Zedillo on Friday, Costa Rican President Jose Maria Figueres on Monday and Dominican President Leonel Fernandez on Tuesday. He has also travelled in the past week to Nicaragua, Panama, El Salvador and Costa Rica, handing over letters from Castro to their leaders. Ferradaz was in Peru this week.

The flurry of activity comes two weeks after Cuba angrily denounced a series of amendments making their way through the U.S. Congress that aim to tighten the Helms Burton law, which came into force in March last year.

Havana has described the moves in Congress as a further assault on Cuba. The U.S. State Department has said there is nothing dramatic about the amendments, which are tacked on to a far wider bill on foreign relations.

According to a copy of Castro's letter released by Costa Rica's government, he lambasted the new U.S. moves against Cuba. "These measures are aimed at reinforcing the economic, financial and commercial blockade (of Cuba) and strengthening the aggressive policies that Washington has maintained for more than 35 years against our country," the letter said.
